section.title: Fight the Good Fight
section.sectionRationale: The letter closes with a stirring personal charge. Timothy, the man of God, is to flee the love of money and pursue godliness, fighting the good fight of the faith until the appearing of Christ, whose coming the blessed and only Sovereign will bring about. Paul adds instructions for the rich to be generous, and a final plea: guard the deposit entrusted to you.
section.thesis: The man of God flees greed and fights the good fight of faith, keeping Christ's command until His appearing, so that the rich hold wealth loosely and generously and the whole trust of the gospel is guarded to the end, to the glory of the blessed and only Sovereign.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the charge to fight the good fight, crowned with the doxology to the blessed and only Sovereign; the charge to the rich to be generous; and the final plea to guard the entrusted deposit.

verses.text: But you, O man of God, flee from these things and pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, perseverance, and gentleness.
{{agonizomai|Fight the good fight}} of the faith. Take hold of the eternal life to which you were called when you made the good {{homologia|confession}} before many witnesses.
I charge you in the presence of God, who gives life to all things, and of Christ Jesus, who made the good confession in His testimony before Pontius Pilate:
Keep this commandment without stain or reproach until the {{epiphaneia|appearance}} of our Lord Jesus Christ,
which the blessed and only {{dynastes|Sovereign One}}, the King of kings and Lord of lords, will bring about in His own time.
He alone is immortal and dwells in unapproachable light. No one has ever seen Him, nor can anyone see Him. To Him be honor and eternal dominion! Amen.
Instruct those who are rich in the present age not to be conceited and not to put their hope in the uncertainty of wealth, but in God, who richly provides all things for us to enjoy.
Instruct them to do good, to be rich in good works, and to be generous and ready to share,
treasuring up for themselves a firm foundation for the future, so that they may take hold of that which is truly life.

units.label: Guard the deposit
units.note: keep the trust to the end

verses.text: O Timothy, guard what has been {{parathede|entrusted}} to you. Avoid irreverent, empty chatter and the opposing arguments of so-called “{{gnosis|knowledge}},”
which some have professed and thus swerved away from the faith. Grace be with you all.

agonizomai.gloss: To contend, struggle, or compete, as in an athletic contest or battle; the root of our word agony. Paired with the noun for a good fight, it pictures the Christian life and ministry as a strenuous contest to be fought with all one's strength, taking hold of eternal life.

homologia.gloss: A confession, an open acknowledgment made with the mouth, literally a saying the same thing. Timothy made the good confession before witnesses, as Christ did before Pilate. Public confession of the faith is a solemn, binding act that shapes the whole of life.

epiphaneia.gloss: An appearing or manifestation, used of the visible coming of Christ; the root of our word epiphany. Timothy is to keep Christ's command spotless until this appearing, giving the whole charge an eye toward the certain return of the Lord in glory.

dynastes.gloss: A ruler, sovereign, or potentate, one who holds power; the root of our word dynasty. God is the blessed and only Sovereign, the King of kings and Lord of lords, whose unrivaled majesty and power will bring about Christ's appearing in His own time.

parathede.gloss: A deposit, something entrusted to another for safekeeping. Timothy is to guard the deposit, the gospel and sound teaching handed to him, keeping it intact and passing it on unspoiled, the letter's final and summarizing charge.

gnosis.gloss: Knowledge. Paul warns against what is falsely called knowledge, the pretentious speculation of the false teachers. The phrase may point to an early form of the error later known as gnosticism; true knowledge is found in the gospel deposit, not in these empty oppositions.

basic.context: Paul makes his final, personal appeal. Timothy, the man of God, must flee the love of money and pursue righteousness and godliness, fighting the good fight of the faith and keeping Christ's command until He appears. This bursts into praise of God, the blessed and only Sovereign, immortal and dwelling in unapproachable light. Paul then tells the rich to be generous and to hope in God, and ends with the charge to guard the gospel entrusted to Timothy.
basic.hermeneutics: The charge is direct and prescriptive: flee greed, pursue godliness, fight for the faith, guard the deposit. The doxology teaches us who God is. The instructions to the rich are timeless wisdom for anyone with means, redirecting hope from wealth to God and calling for generosity.
basic.originalLanguages: Timothy is to agonizomai, fight the good fight, having made the good homologia, confession. He keeps the command until the epiphaneia, appearing, of Christ, which the blessed dynastes, Sovereign, will bring. His last task is to guard the parathede, deposit, against what is falsely called gnosis, knowledge.
basic.typology: The good confession before Pilate marks Christ as the faithful witness whose testimony Timothy's own confession echoes. The King of kings and Lord of lords, veiled here in unapproachable light, is fully revealed in Christ at His appearing.
basic.christ: Christ made the good confession before Pontius Pilate, standing as the faithful witness Timothy is to imitate. The whole charge looks to His epiphaneia, His glorious appearing, which the sovereign God will bring about in His own time. The gospel of Christ is the very deposit Timothy must guard to the end.
basic.god: God is the blessed and only Sovereign, the King of kings and Lord of lords, alone immortal, dwelling in unapproachable light, unseen and unseeable, worthy of honor and eternal dominion. He gives life to all things and richly provides all we enjoy. He is the great reality that dwarfs the love of money and steadies the fight of faith.
basic.crossReferences: Second Timothy 4 records Paul's own finished fight and kept faith. Revelation 19 names Christ King of kings and Lord of lords. Matthew 6 tells us to store up treasure in heaven, echoing the charge to the rich.
basic.oneStory: The whole letter, and the whole Bible, aims at the day when the blessed and only Sovereign brings Christ's appearing. Timothy is charged to fight and to guard the gospel until then. His faithfulness belongs to God's long work of keeping His truth alive across the generations until the King of kings is revealed in glory.

context.literary:
This is the letter's last movement, and it gathers up almost every thread. The opening 'But you' in verse 11 answers the men of the previous verses, the money-lovers who wander and are pierced, and sets Timothy against them. The charge is then built around two commands to flee and pursue in verse 11, two commands to fight and take hold in verse 12, and a solemn 'I charge you' in verse 13 that carries one long sentence through verse 16. The sentence ends not with a command but with praise, so that the charge dissolves into a doxology. The whole letter thus ends where it began, since 1:17 is also a doxology to the King eternal, immortal and invisible, and the two together frame the letter in praise.

Two witnesses stand in the middle of the charge. In verse 12 Timothy made the good confession before many witnesses, and in verse 13 Christ made the good confession before Pontius Pilate. The same noun and the same adjective bind them. Timothy's confession is placed in the light of Christ's. The only secular name in the passage is Pilate's, and it is there for a reason: he fixes the story in history, as the creeds later do.

The second section, verses 17 to 19, returns to wealth, so that the passage finishes the argument begun in 6:5 to 10. The rich are not told to be poor but to hope in God and to be generous. The last section, verses 20 and 21, is brief and urgent: guard the deposit, avoid empty talk. The closing blessing is plural, 'Grace be with you all,' which shows that the letter was meant to be read to the church and not only to Timothy.
context.historical:
The title 'man of God' was an old one. In the Old Testament it was given to Moses, Deuteronomy 33:1, and to prophets and others who spoke for God. To call Timothy by it, at the close of the letter, places him in line with those who carried God's word, and Paul uses it again in 2 Timothy 3:17. The charge also draws on the world of athletic contests, familiar to a Greek-speaking city, in which the same word for a contest or struggle stands for any hard-fought effort. Paul uses the same picture of himself in 2 Timothy 4:7, where he says he has fought the good fight.

The confession before witnesses may refer to Timothy's baptism or to the occasion of his commissioning, which is described in 1:18 and 4:14. The mention of Pilate recalls the trial of Jesus, Mark 15:2 and John 18:36 to 37, where He confirmed He was a king while saying His kingdom was not from this world. The line of the letter 'King of kings and Lord of lords' would also have sounded against the claims made for rulers. The Greek word for appearing, epiphaneia, was used in the Greek world for the visible arrival of a god or of a king in a city, so the believers would have heard that the real arrival is still to come.

Ephesus was wealthy. The instruction to the rich assumes some church members were well off, as the letter also shows in 2:9 to 10. Their danger was not only greed but pride and false security, and Paul does not ask them to give up their property. The warning about 'so-called knowledge' belongs to a setting where clever teaching, speculation and endless genealogies were circulating, as 1:3 to 4 shows.
context.canonical:
The doxology of verses 15 and 16 weaves the Old Testament together. God as 'God of gods and Lord of lords' is from Deuteronomy 10:17, and Daniel 2:47 says He is the God of gods and Lord of kings. In Revelation the title is given to the Lamb, who is Lord of lords and King of kings, Revelation 17:14, and written on the rider's robe at His return, Revelation 19:16. Paul assigns the title to God here, and John assigns it to Christ, and together they show how the New Testament holds the Father and the Son in the same honour.

That no one has seen God or can see Him matches Exodus 33:20, where Moses is told he cannot see God's face and live, and John 1:18, where the Son has made the unseen God known. That God dwells in light matches Psalm 104:2, where He wraps Himself in light, and the end of the Bible, where there is no night in the city and the Lord God is its light, Revelation 22:5.

Timothy's charge is repeated in Paul's own last words. In 2 Timothy 4:7 to 8 he says he has fought the good fight, finished the race and kept the faith, and awaits a crown for those who love Christ's appearing. The deposit appears again in 2 Timothy 1:14 and 2:2, where the treasure is entrusted to faithful men who will teach others. The charge to the rich draws on Jesus' teaching to store up treasure in heaven, Luke 12:33, and on His saying that it is more blessed to give than to receive, Acts 20:35.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul wanted Timothy to end the letter on his feet. After pages of instruction on order, widows, elders and false teaching, he wanted the young man to hear that the real matter is a contest of faith to be fought with the whole person, and that the fight is carried by a vision of God. This is why the charge slides into a doxology. Timothy is not left with a list of tasks but with a picture of the King whom he serves, and who will appear at the right time.

Paul also wanted the rich in the church to be dealt with fairly. He does not condemn them for having property, and he does not flatter them. He tells Timothy to instruct them not to be conceited, not to trust in what is uncertain, but to trust the God who gives, and to use their money for good works. Finally he wanted the church to understand that the gospel is a deposit, entrusted from God through Paul to Timothy to others. It is guarded, not reinvented, and the guard consists of both holding it and refusing the quarrelsome speculation that undermines it.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The imperatives are plain, and they apply to any servant of Christ: flee the love of money and its company, pursue the six qualities of verse 11, fight, take hold, keep the commandment, guard the deposit. Some details belong to Timothy's own case. The confession before many witnesses refers to his own commissioning, and the charge in the presence of God and Christ is directed to him as Paul's delegate. A believer today does not repeat the ceremony but takes the same stance.

The instruction to the rich is also a direct word, and it is not limited to the very wealthy. 'Rich in the present age' is relative, and anyone who has more than enough must hear it. It says what to do with wealth: hope in God, do good, be generous, share. It does not tell the rich to give everything away, though Jesus told one man to do so in Mark 10:21. The two fit together, since Jesus dealt with a particular man whose possessions had a hold on him. The doxology describes who God is and is not a command, yet it governs the whole passage.

debates.question: What was the 'good confession before many witnesses' in verse 12?

views.label: Timothy's baptism
views.case: Baptism was the public declaration of faith in Jesus, and the 'eternal life to which you were called' fits the moment a believer first confesses Christ. The many witnesses would be the congregation present.

views.label: Timothy's commissioning for ministry
views.case: The letter speaks elsewhere of prophecies over Timothy and a laying on of hands, 1:18 and 4:14. The setting would then be the occasion when he was set apart, before the elders and the church.

views.label: A general confession of faith, perhaps at both
views.case: Some hold that the phrase is not tied to one event and describes the confession that every believer makes and that Timothy had made publicly more than once. It sets his life against Christ's good confession before Pilate.

debates.bearing: The point does not depend on the occasion. Timothy has publicly bound himself to Christ, and the charge calls him to live up to what he said before others.

debates.question: Who is the 'blessed and only Sovereign' in verses 15 and 16?

views.label: God the Father
views.case: The sentence says Christ's appearing is something this Sovereign will bring about, which suggests a distinction. The description 'alone immortal' and 'no one has ever seen Him' matches how the letter speaks of God in 1:17, and verse 13 distinguishes God from Christ.

views.label: Christ himself
views.case: The title King of kings and Lord of lords is given to Christ in Revelation 17:14 and 19:16, and the Greek is not explicit about the antecedent of 'His own time.' Some therefore take the doxology as praise of Christ.

views.label: The one God, without separating the persons
views.case: A third group holds that Paul is praising God in his unity, and that Christian teaching later sets the Father and the Son within this glory, as Revelation shows when it applies the same titles to the Lamb.

debates.bearing: The structure favours the Father, who will bring about the appearing of the Son. Yet the same title in Revelation shows that the Son shares the Father's honour, so the doxology cannot be used against the deity of Christ.

debates.question: What is the 'so-called knowledge' of verse 20?

views.label: An early form of the movement later called Gnosticism
views.case: The word for knowledge is gnosis, and the verse speaks of opposing arguments that claim it. Many scholars connect this with the speculative teaching that the letters oppose in 1:3 to 7 and that prized secret knowledge.

views.label: Jewish or mixed speculation about the law and genealogies
views.case: The letter's earlier mentions of myths, genealogies and the law, 1:4 and 1:7, suggest a teaching that had a Jewish colour and was not yet the later system. The label 'so-called' says the claim to knowledge is false whatever its form.

views.label: Any clever teaching that sets itself against the gospel
views.case: Others read the phrase as a general warning against anything that markets itself as deeper insight and displaces the deposit. Paul writes to Timothy and also to later readers.

debates.bearing: The precise label matters less than the test. Whatever calls itself knowledge but leads away from the faith is to be refused, and the deposit is the measure.

study.originalLanguages:
The charge opens with 'man of God,' anthropos theou, and the contrast with 'these things' is sharp. The verb 'flee' is pheugo, the same word Paul uses for sexual immorality in 1 Corinthians 6:18 and for idolatry in 1 Corinthians 10:14, and the companion verb 'pursue' is dioko, which elsewhere describes a hunter chasing prey or a persecutor chasing the church. In 2 Timothy 2:22 the same pair appears again with different objects. The six objects of pursuit in verse 11 are righteousness, godliness, faith, love, perseverance and gentleness. The fifth word, hypomone, means steadfast endurance under pressure, and the sixth, praotes, is the strength that holds back, and the last pair makes a deliberate counterweight: Timothy must be strong enough to endure and gentle enough not to hurt.

Verse 12 gives 'Fight the good fight,' agonizomai ton kalon agona, in which the verb and noun share a root, so the English is close: contest the good contest. The word for 'good' is kalos, which in the Pastorals describes what is noble and attractive, and it is attached to fight, confession, foundation and deeds. 'Take hold' is epilambanomai, the verb of grasping, and the same verb returns in verse 19 as 'take hold of that which is truly life.' In verse 19 the phrase 'truly life' uses the same adverb ontos as the 'truly widows' of 5:3, and in both places the word separates the real from the counterfeit.

The confession of verses 12 and 13 shares a word, homologia, the noun for saying the same thing, agreeing, professing. Christ's is a 'testimony,' from martyreo, to bear witness, from which English takes martyr. In verse 13 God is 'who gives life to all things,' zoogoneo, to keep alive or give life, which is the word used in the Septuagint for preserving life. In verse 14 Timothy is to keep the commandment 'without stain or reproach,' aspilos and anepilemptos, which together say that he is to be unspotted and beyond blame. 'Appearance' is epiphaneia, used in the Pastorals for both comings of Christ, 2 Timothy 1:10 and Titus 2:13. 'In His own time' is literally 'in His own seasons,' plural, so God has fixed times for His acts.

In verse 15 the word for 'Sovereign' is dynastes, a ruler with power. The two titles that follow are built from participles, 'the one reigning over those who reign,' and 'the one ruling over those who rule,' which adds action to the titles taken from Deuteronomy 10:17. In verse 17 the rich are told not to be 'conceited,' literally not to think high thoughts, and the opposite, to be 'rich in good works,' sets a different currency against wealth. The word for what Timothy must guard, paratheke, means something placed in trust with another. In 2 Timothy 1:14 Paul uses a related command. In verse 20 'opposing arguments' is antitheseis, which also means contradictions. Verse 21 ends with 'Grace be with you,' and the pronoun is plural.

typology.type: The man of God and the contest
typology.fulfillment: Moses, Samuel, Elijah and others are called men of God, those who spoke and stood for the LORD against opposition. Timothy is placed in that line. In Christ the office reaches its centre. He is the Prophet like Moses, Deuteronomy 18:15, who stands before Pilate and testifies to the truth, John 18:37. Timothy's fight is derivative and supported, and he fights because Christ has already won, John 16:33. The type falls short where the prophets sometimes failed, as Moses did at Meribah, and Christ never did.

A deposit left with a trusted person recalls the covenant documents and the ark where Israel's testimony was kept, Deuteronomy 31:26. The gospel is the greater deposit. It was entrusted to the apostles, and from them to faithful men who teach others, 2 Timothy 2:2. In Christ the deposit is not only words but a Person, and it is guarded with the help of the Holy Spirit, 2 Timothy 1:14. The picture falls short if guarding sounds like keeping something inert. The deposit is alive, and it is kept by the Spirit as much as by the guardian.

typology.type: Treasure laid up as a foundation
typology.fulfillment: The rich are told to treasure up a good foundation for the future. The image echoes Proverbs, where wealth makes wings for itself and flies away, Proverbs 23:5, and where righteousness is a lasting foundation. In Christ the teaching reaches its source. He said to provide purses that will not wear out, an inexhaustible treasure in heaven, Luke 12:33, and Paul says the foundation is Christ Himself, 1 Corinthians 3:11. The type falls short if generosity is treated as a way of buying heaven; the good works are fruit and not the price.

study.christ:
The passage leads to Christ most directly in verse 13, where He is the one 'who made the good confession in His testimony before Pontius Pilate.' Pilate asked whether He was a king, and Jesus said that His kingdom was not of this world and that He had come into the world to testify to the truth, John 18:36 to 37. The Roman governor had power of life and death, and Jesus answered plainly. Timothy is pressed to see his own confession in that light. Whatever resistance he faces, Christ faced the strongest earthly power and did not alter His testimony. The sentence also fixes the faith in history, since Pilate was governor of Judea and the death of Jesus is as real as that.

It leads to Christ in the expectation of verse 14. The whole charge is held until the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ. The word epiphaneia was used for the arrival of a ruler, and Paul has already used it of Christ's first coming in 2 Timothy 1:10 and uses it of His return in Titus 2:13, where he calls it the blessed hope and glorious appearance of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ. The whole of Timothy's labour has a destination. The sentence holds out a day on which the One who was tried before Pilate will be seen by all.

It leads to Christ in the titles of verse 15. 'King of kings and Lord of lords' is given to God in Deuteronomy 10:17 and to the Lamb in Revelation 17:14 and 19:16. Here Paul gives it to the one who brings about the appearing, and John gives it to the one who appears, so the New Testament does not keep the titles apart. The glory that is unapproachable in verse 16 is, according to John 1:18, made known by the Son, who is at the Father's side. The God whom no one has seen can be known, because Christ has made Him known.

It leads to Christ through the contrast of the rich and the poor. Christ, who was rich, became poor, 2 Corinthians 8:9. The command to the rich to be generous echoes His call to a rich man to sell and give, Mark 10:21, and His word that it is more blessed to give than to receive, Acts 20:35. The treasure that the rich are told to lay up is the treasure He promised in Luke 12:33.

A caution: the deposit and the fight are not secret codes for Christ, and the passage should not be read as if every phrase is a hidden picture of Him. The links rest on what the apostles say. What the chapter gives is Christ as the pattern of confession, the object of expectation, and the one who bears the titles of the sovereign God.
study.god:
The doxology is one of the fullest descriptions of God in Paul's letters, and each phrase carries its weight. God is 'blessed,' meaning His happiness is complete in Himself, with no lack that creatures must supply. He is the 'only Sovereign,' with no rival and no equal, and His rule is not shared with any other power. He is King of kings and Lord of lords, so that every human ruler, including Pilate and the emperors, is a subordinate. The title is borrowed from Deuteronomy 10:17 and widened by the verbs of ruling so that God is shown reigning at this moment over those who think they reign.

God is 'alone immortal.' All other life is derived, and He alone has life in Himself. This is why verse 13 can speak of Him as the one who gives life to all things. The sentence matters for the whole passage, since a believer who knows that life comes from God does not need to cling to wealth to hold on to it. It also matters for the fight, because Timothy is asked to take hold of eternal life, which only the immortal One can give.

God 'dwells in unapproachable light,' and no one has seen or can see Him. This is a reminder of God's holiness and otherness, set beside the nearness of verse 17, in which He richly provides all things for us to enjoy. The same God who is beyond sight is the God who gives food and the pleasure of it. The doctrine of God has to keep both: the distance that makes worship possible and the generosity that makes thanks possible.

God is a God of times. The appearing will come 'in His own time,' not by human scheme. The Sovereign is neither hurried nor late. The believer who is called to fight is also called to wait, and the waiting is trust in a God who has fixed the seasons.

God is the generous giver in verse 17. He does not forbid enjoyment, which is again the point of 4:3 to 5, and He is the proper object of hope in place of wealth. The generosity He asks of the rich is a copy of His own character.

For worship, the passage invites the church to praise, as the apostle himself does. The doxology breaks into the middle of instruction because the instruction is for the sake of the One who is praised. The words 'honor and eternal dominion' are an offering, and the 'Amen' is the church's agreement.

crossReferences.note: Paul says he has fought the good fight, finished the race and kept the faith. He is now where he wants Timothy to be. The same words that he asked Timothy to take up in 1 Timothy 6:12 are used by Paul of his own life, so that the charge is also a testimony.

Paul tells Timothy to guard the treasure entrusted to him, with the help of the Holy Spirit who dwells in us. The command repeats the 'deposit' of 1 Timothy 6:20 and adds that the guarding is not done in Timothy's strength alone.

Paul tells Timothy to flee youthful passions and pursue righteousness, faith, love and peace. The pair of verbs is the same as in 1 Timothy 6:11, and the repetition suggests that fleeing and pursuing belong together in Timothy's ordinary discipline.

Jesus tells Pilate that He was born and came into the world to testify to the truth. This is the good confession that Paul has in mind in 1 Timothy 6:13. It shows that Christ's testimony was a King's witness in a court, spoken to the highest authority present.

The LORD is God of gods and Lord of lords, showing no partiality and accepting no bribe. The title in 1 Timothy 6:15 comes from here, and the surrounding words about partiality and bribes fit Paul's earlier instructions about bias and about money.

The returning Christ has a name written on His robe, King of kings and Lord of lords. The title Paul gives to God in the doxology is given to Christ at His appearing, which is the very event that the doxology expects.

God tells Moses that no one can see His face and live. This is the background of the statement that no one has seen or can see God. The verse shows why the doxology speaks of unapproachable light and why a mediator is needed.
No one has ever seen God, but the one and only Son has made Him known. The text answers the problem that Paul states in verse 16. The unseen God is not unknowable, because the Son has shown Him.

Jesus tells His followers to sell their possessions and give to the poor and to provide purses that will not wear out. The advice is the teaching behind verses 18 and 19, where the rich are told to treasure up a firm foundation for the future.

Paul quotes the Lord Jesus, 'It is more blessed to give than to receive.' The sentence gives the positive reason for the generosity in 1 Timothy 6:18, since giving is the way the rich take hold of what is truly life.

The letter's first doxology praises the King eternal, immortal and invisible, the only God. The final doxology repeats these themes and enlarges them, so the letter is framed by praise, and the instruction in between is the way of life that belongs to such a God.

study.oneStory:
The first temptation in Eden was to doubt God's word and to grasp at what He had held back, and the human race has been fighting that battle since. Paul calls Timothy to fight on the right side of it. The language of contest picks up the larger story in which the seed of the woman struggles against the serpent, Genesis 3:15, and the church is drawn into the same struggle, as Paul says in Ephesians 6:12, though the weapons are righteousness, faith and love.

The doxology steps back and shows who rules the story. Pharaoh, Nebuchadnezzar, Caesar and Pilate all appear in it, and the Lord is God of gods and Lord of lords, Deuteronomy 10:17, who humbles kings, Daniel 2:47. The passage asserts that this is true even when the church is small and under pressure. It also teaches that the appearing of Christ is not something that happens by accident but is brought about by God in His own time, as the whole of Scripture moves toward it.

The deposit belongs to the story of how God's word is carried. It passes from the prophets to Christ, from Christ to the apostles, and from the apostles to faithful men who teach others, 2 Timothy 2:2. Each generation guards what it has received and hands it on. The church is not the author of the gospel but its steward. The warning against so-called knowledge is a reminder that the story has always been attacked by clever substitutes, from the serpent's promise of knowledge in Genesis 3:5 on.

The passage closes the letter by pointing at a future that has both a fight and a rest. Timothy is told to take hold of eternal life, and the rich are told to take hold of what is truly life. The Bible ends with the God who dwells in light made visible, the servants who see His face, and the city in which there is no night because the Lord God is its light, Revelation 22:4 to 5. The One who was unseen will be seen, and the fight will end in the sight of the King.

quiz.q: What is Timothy, as a man of God, told to flee and to pursue?

options.text: Flee the love of money; pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, perseverance, and gentleness.
options.note: Verse 11 gives both the flight and the pursuit.

options.text: Flee all hardship; pursue a comfortable life.
options.note: He is called to fight, not to seek comfort; the pursuit is godliness, not ease.

options.text: Flee other believers; pursue solitude.
options.note: The flight is from greed and its evils, not from the church.

options.text: Flee doctrine; pursue personal freedom.
options.note: He is to guard doctrine, not flee it.

quiz.q: What does Paul mean by fight the good fight of the faith?

options.text: To contend earnestly for the faith and take hold of eternal life.
options.note: Verse 12 casts the Christian life as a strenuous contest with an eternal prize.

options.text: To start quarrels with everyone who disagrees.
options.note: It is a fight for the faith and toward godliness, not mere quarreling.

options.text: To win political power for the church.
options.note: The fight is for faith and eternal life, not earthly power.

options.text: To avoid all struggle and coast along.
options.note: The image is a demanding contest, the opposite of coasting.

quiz.q: How does Paul describe God in the doxology of verses 15 and 16?

options.text: The blessed and only Sovereign, King of kings and Lord of lords, alone immortal, dwelling in unapproachable light.
options.note: Verses 15 and 16 give this majestic praise.

options.text: One ruler among many rival powers.
options.note: He is the only Sovereign, the King of kings, not one among rivals.

options.text: A being fully visible to all who look.
options.note: Paul says no one has seen Him nor can see Him.

options.text: A distant deity with no involvement in the world.
options.note: He gives life to all things and will bring about Christ's appearing.

quiz.q: What is Paul's charge to those who are rich?

options.text: Not to trust in wealth but in God, and to be generous and rich in good works.
options.note: Verses 17 to 19 redirect their hope and call for generosity.

options.text: To feel guilty and give away everything at once.
options.note: He calls for generosity and right hope, not guilt-driven abandonment; God gives all things to enjoy.

options.text: To enjoy wealth with no thought for others.
options.note: They are to be generous and ready to share, not self-indulgent.

options.text: To put their full confidence in their riches.
options.note: Their hope is to be in God, not in uncertain wealth.

quiz.q: What is Paul's final charge to Timothy?

options.text: Guard what has been entrusted to you, avoiding empty chatter and false knowledge.
options.note: Verse 20 gives the closing charge to guard the deposit.

options.text: Pursue the latest speculative knowledge.
options.note: He is to avoid what is falsely called knowledge, not chase it.

options.text: Keep the gospel to himself.
options.note: He guards it to keep it intact and pass it on, not to hoard it.

options.text: Abandon the faith if it becomes difficult.
options.note: He is to guard the faith to the end, warning against those who swerved from it.

questions: Paul calls Timothy to both flee and pursue. What specifically do you most need to flee right now, and what should you be running toward instead?
The Christian life is a good fight, not a stroll. Where are you fighting well for the faith, and where have you gone passive?
The doxology lifts our eyes to the blessed and only Sovereign. How does a bigger vision of God shrink the things that tempt and frighten you?
The rich are told to hope in God, not wealth, and to be generous. Whatever your means, where is your hope quietly resting, and how generous are you?
Timothy was to guard the deposit of the gospel. What has been entrusted to you to keep and pass on faithfully, and how are you guarding it?

translationNotes.note: Fight the good fight renders a noun and verb from the same root, agon, picturing a strenuous athletic or military contest, echoed in 2 Timothy 4:7.
So-called knowledge translates a phrase, falsely named knowledge, gnosis; many see here an early form of the error later called gnosticism.
The BSB footnote notes that some manuscripts add Amen at the very end of the letter.
